name: Colin Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Colin. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me is confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage Ladyfield Farm with my dad. We rent it from the Carrow Estate: 180 hectares of wheat and sugar beet, about 50 beef cattle, and we buy in 400 store lambs each autumn to fatten on the beet tops. My dad's sixty-one with a bad back, so most days it's me on the tractor, me in the cattle shed, and him on the phone to the grain merchant.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like building something that's ours, even if the land isn't. What wears me out is that Dad pays me what the farm can afford, which isn't much, and I've got about three weeks of savings. And the tenancy, which is our rental agreement with the estate, comes up for renewal in 2029, and the estate's land agent has been taking farms back to run with contractors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. I'd be glad, honestly. We've got enough to worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, farming stays farming. At the young farmers' club I'd say it's about hard work, not apps. I'd maybe share a joke online, but nothing serious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it changes nothing about 2029. The estate could still take Ladyfield back and farm it with a contractor, AI or no AI. That's the thing that keeps me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the farm running as tight as we can and save what I can, maybe a hundred a month. I'd take on hedge-cutting contracts with our tractor in winter for extra money. And I'd start getting our accounts in order to show the estate we're good tenants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried about 2029. Not about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would losing the tenancy mean for you and your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd mean losing the house as well as the work, because the farmhouse comes with the tenancy. Dad would retire to my aunt's, probably. I'd have to find work on someone else's farm, and there aren't many around here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you feel about the estate taking farms back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's their land, they've every right. But it's hard to watch families who've farmed there for sixty years get a letter. If the Carrow Estate wants the land back in 2029, three generations of Fischers are out with a letter.

think: It **changes nothing** about the 2029 tenancy renewal.
The estate could still **take Ladyfield back** with a contractor.
do: Get the **accounts in order** to impress the estate.

fieldNote: His real risk is the **tenancy renewal**, already real before AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one sounds likely. And I can see how it'd go for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good for farms that use it, and I'd mean it. At the club I'd say we should learn the tools, not fight them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it worries me, because it makes it easier for the estate to farm Ladyfield themselves. An AI can plan crops and order fertiliser for a contractor, and that makes a tenant farmer like me less needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use AI more for planning and the farm accounts, so we look sharp to the estate. I'd join the Tenant Farmers' Association, which argues for tenants' rights. I'd keep the hedge-cutting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I'd be busy, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your dad does the phone and the merchant. How would he cope with AI doing some of that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad would hate it, at first. But he'd come round once I showed him a better price on the wheat. He's a businessman under the moaning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the land agent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the land agent we're the best tenants he's got, and show him the numbers. I'd ask for a longer tenancy, ten years. Worst he can say is no.

fieldNote: He sees AI as **strengthening the landlord's hand**.

steps.text: Use AI for Ladyfield's crop plans and accounts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028, then robots by 2031. That lines up badly with our tenancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to stand on their own feet, but this is too fast for anyone. I'd say it at the club and to our MP.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the estate would take Ladyfield back in 2029 and run it with AI and contractors, then robots after 2031. Dad would retire, and I'd be twenty-nine with no farm and no house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the Tenant Farmers' Association straight away and push for longer tenancies by law. I'd talk to Dad about using his small savings to help me rent some land elsewhere. If it fell through, I'd move to my cousin's farm in the north.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the floor's dropping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap between the AI and the robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, because our trouble starts in 2029, right in the middle. The estate doesn't need robots to take our farm, because AI and a contractor will do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept help from the government?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rather not. I'd take help from family first. But if it was that or losing everything, I'd swallow my pride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, robots by 2034. That gives us a bit more of a chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say now's the time for farms to get ahead. I'd say it at the club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the tenancy renewal in 2029 is before AGI here. If we can get a longer tenancy then, we might be all right. If not, we're in trouble either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the AI tools properly before 2029 and use them to show the estate we're efficient. I'd join a machinery ring, which is a group of farms that share equipment, so we could share a robot later. And I'd save every spare penny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever buy a robot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once a few farms around us had one working, yes. I'm not going to be first. But if robots are the future, I want to own one, not be replaced by one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your dad think of all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad says it's all nonsense, but he's watching. He's started asking me what the AI says about wheat prices. That's progress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a fair run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farmers who prepare will be fine. I'd tell people to get their house in order now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think we could make it. If we win a longer tenancy in 2029, I'd have ten years to build up, and maybe buy a robot before 2039. The estate would need good tenants who know the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push for a longer tenancy in 2029, save hard, and learn the AI tools as they're proven. I'd join a machinery ring and look at sharing a robot around 2037.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but hopeful. It's a long road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your own life beyond the farm, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to settle down, marry, maybe have kids by then. With ten years, I'd feel I could settle down and have kids, but with two, I wouldn't dare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Dad that Ladyfield has a future if we're smart. I'd want him to see the farm go on with a Fischer on it. That's what matters to him.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because our tenancy renewal falls right in the gap. What would help is secure, longer tenancies by law, so landlords can't just swap families for contractors. And cheap loans for small farms to buy into robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about what a farm is. Ladyfield (the family farm) isn't just a business, it's a family. If the robots run it, it's just land.
